definition: Ascribe means to assign or credit to a cause or source.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ascribe. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ascribe should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Fans ascribe the team's turnaround to its new goalkeeper, though the schedule softened at exactly the same moment.
Suspect is much fainter than ascribe — a suspected cause is merely wondered about, nothing assigned yet, while to ascribe is to write the effect down to its cause openly, on the record.
Pin goes further than ascribe — an ascribed cause can still be argued; a fault pinned on someone is treated as settled.

Attribute is the everyday twin — to attribute is to assign an effect to a cause in plain conversation. Ascribe does the same assigning in a more scholarly register, where causes and sources get argued over, and it wears uncertainty comfortably: a painting ascribed to a workshop may yet be reassigned.

Credit assigns a cause too, but only for outcomes worth having — you credit the striker with the win, never with the loss. Ascribe holds the scales level: good, bad, or merely odd, an effect can be ascribed to any source without praising or blaming anyone.

Impute assigns a cause or motive with a finger pointed — faults, motives, and blame get imputed. Ascribe keeps the accusation out of it: a result can be ascribed to any source, innocent or not, while an imputed motive always carries a suspicion of wrongdoing.

Ascribe means to assign or credit to a cause or source.
The sourdough came out tangier every winter, and for years the baker ascribed the difference to her starter, a jar older than the shop itself.

Then a friend boarded up the drafty cellar window as a favor, the tang mellowed in January for the first time, and the jar kept its reputation for nothing: the cold, not the culture, had been setting the flavor all along.
Ascribe is the exact word for what the baker did, because ascribe means to assign or credit to a cause or source — she wrote the tang down to the jar, rightly or not.
Blame works only when the outcome is bad, credit only when it is good; ascribe stays neutral.
And as the baker learned, an ascription is a claim, not a proof.
Ascribe is the historian's and critic's verb, at home where causes and sources are argued over.
Attribute, met among this unit's reference words, is its everyday twin; credit leans positive and blame negative, while ascribe holds the scales level.
It also suits shaky assignments — paintings ascribed to a workshop, sayings ascribed to the wrong sage — wherever the assignment itself might be wrong.

For decades, historians could not explain why the summer of 1816 failed across three continents at once — frost in June, harvests dead in the field, grain prices tripling from Vermont to Bengal.
The written records blamed everything local: a cursed valley here, a neglected saint's day there.

Then tree-ring scientists matched a razor-thin growth ring in oaks on both sides of the Atlantic to ash layers in polar ice, and the field began to ascribe the global crop failure to a single event — the eruption of Mount Tambora the year before.
The attribution remains, strictly speaking, provisional; no written source connects the two, and the argument runs entirely through physical evidence.
But each new ice core has thickened the case rather than thinned it.
